scenes.tts: The first film showed how chromosome copies reach matching nuclei. How can a frozen onion root reveal which part of that cycle takes longest? The cells cannot answer, but their patterns can.
scenes.visual: Hook before title. Reuse the first film's COLOR MAP exactly: chromosome pairs BLUE/LIGHT BLUE and ORANGE/LIGHT ORANGE, spindle fibers GREEN, nuclear envelopes YELLOW, cell boundaries TEAL, labels TEXT. Show the final matching nuclei from the first film shrinking into cells near an onion root tip. Freeze the moving root and stamp a large question mark over a microscope field.
scenes.narration: The first film showed how chromosome copies reach matching nuclei. How can a frozen onion root reveal which part of that cycle takes longest? The cells cannot answer, but their patterns can.

scenes.visual: Brief title card after the hook: A Snapshot Becomes a Clock. A circular clock outline transforms into a round microscope field. No subtitle.

scenes.tts: A stained root tip is a snapshot. Each cell is caught at one moment of its cycle. Some show loose chromosomes inside a yellow nucleus. Others show chromosomes coiling, lining up, separating, or reaching opposite ends.
scenes.visual: Fill the frame with a schematic microscope field of varied rectangular onion cells. Animate all cells cycling, then freeze them together. In sequence, spotlight an interphase nucleus, a prophase cell, a metaphase row, an anaphase split and a telophase pair. Label the entire field schematic.
scenes.narration: A stained root tip is a snapshot. Each cell is caught at one moment of its cycle. Some show loose chromosomes inside a yellow nucleus. Others show chromosomes coiling, lining up, separating, or reaching opposite ends.

scenes.tts: Imagine many runners photographed at random points around a track. A slow section holds more runners because each runner stays there longer. Cycling cells follow the same counting model. A longer phase should appear in more cells.
scenes.visual: Transform the microscope field into a circular track divided into phase-colored arcs. Simple cell icons travel around it at a steady schematic pace. Stretch one arc while icons continue moving; more icons collect within that arc. Transform the track back into the root-tip field without changing icon positions.
scenes.narration: Imagine many runners photographed at random points around a track. A slow section holds more runners because each runner stays there longer. Cycling cells follow the same counting model. A longer phase should appear in more cells.

scenes.tts: Two phase lanes now contain different numbers of cells. Suppose every cycling cell moves steadily and the sample is fair. Which lane represents the longer-lasting phase? Hold your answer.
scenes.visual: Sort the cell icons into two large unlabeled lanes. Put visibly more cells in the left lane. Show the assumptions as two checked cards: fair sample; steady cycling. Keep the lane labels hidden and the cell icons gently bobbing.
scenes.narration: Two phase lanes now contain different numbers of cells. Suppose every cycling cell moves steadily and the sample is fair. Which lane represents the longer-lasting phase? Hold your answer.

scenes.visual: Deliberate thinking pause. Keep both lanes, the assumptions and the question visible. Pulse the lane brackets, but do not reveal the answer.

scenes.tts: The fuller lane represents the longer phase. More cells were caught there because each one remains there longer. This gives a fraction, not a stopwatch reading. Divide the cells in one phase by all the cells counted, assuming every one is cycling.
scenes.visual: Reveal LONGER under the fuller lane. Compress both lanes into a fraction bar: cells in phase over all cells counted. Use cell icons rather than spoken arithmetic. Then morph the fraction bar into the matching fraction of a circular cycle.
scenes.narration: The fuller lane represents the longer phase. More cells were caught there because each one remains there longer. This gives a fraction, not a stopwatch reading. Divide the cells in one phase by all the cells counted, assuming every one is cycling.

scenes.tts: Now sort one teaching set by visible clues. Intact nuclei go to interphase. Coiled chromosomes go to prophase. A middle row marks metaphase. Separating groups mark anaphase. Two forming nuclei mark telophase.
scenes.visual: Bring in the lesson's teaching-set field and label it schematic reconstruction. Move each rectangular cell into five named bins. Reuse the same chromosome, spindle and envelope drawings from the first film. Show the lesson counts as digits above the bins, never in narration: interphase 20, prophase 10, metaphase 3, anaphase 2, telophase 1; total 36.
scenes.narration: Now sort one teaching set by visible clues. Intact nuclei go to interphase. Coiled chromosomes go to prophase. A middle row marks metaphase. Separating groups mark anaphase. Two forming nuclei mark telophase.

scenes.tts: To estimate time, multiply a phase's fraction by the total cycle time. The teaching activity supplies a round total time rather than measuring it. Put that value on screen. The result is a model estimate for this set.
scenes.visual: Transform one phase fraction into a segment on a full-cycle bar. On screen only: "24 h = 1,440 min (assumed)" and "time in a phase = fraction x 1,440 min". Leave the five phase estimates as blank boxes; the lesson asks students to compute them. Animate the five phase segments joining into one complete bar. Add the label model estimate beneath the bar.
scenes.narration: To estimate time, multiply a phase's fraction by the total cycle time. The teaching activity supplies a round total time rather than measuring it. Put that value on screen. The result is a model estimate for this set.

scenes.tts: The model can fail if the pictures were chosen to display every stage. It also weakens if cells stopped cycling or changed pace. A random field, a clear sampling rule, and a measured total time would support stronger estimates.
scenes.visual: Show three failure modes one at a time while clearing the previous one: a hand selecting dramatic mitotic cells; some cells leaving the cycle; a speed dial changing. Replace them with three stronger-design icons: random field grid, written sampling path, measured clock. Keep all labels under five words.
scenes.narration: The model can fail if the pictures were chosen to display every stage. It also weakens if cells stopped cycling or changed pace. A random field, a clear sampling rule, and a measured total time would support stronger estimates.

scenes.tts: One more distinction matters. Mitosis separates chromosomes between nuclei, while cytokinesis separates the cell. Root-tip photographs can show both nearby, but the phase count sorts chromosome patterns. It does not directly time membrane or wall completion. The two processes overlap, so one snapshot can catch both.
scenes.visual: Split one root-tip cell diagram into two linked tracks. On the upper track, BLUE chromosomes enter YELLOW nuclei under MITOSIS. On the lower track, a TEAL cell plate grows under CYTOKINESIS. Overlap the tracks on one timeline, then point the phase-count bracket only to the chromosome-pattern track.
scenes.narration: One more distinction matters. Mitosis separates chromosomes between nuclei, while cytokinesis separates the cell. Root-tip photographs can show both nearby, but the phase count sorts chromosome patterns. It does not directly time membrane or wall completion. The two processes overlap, so one snapshot can catch both.

scenes.tts: The count still teaches an important idea. Cells spend time growing, copying D N A, and preparing before chromosomes visibly separate. That preparation serves the first film's rule. Copy each chromosome first; separate the copies so each nucleus gets one. And the counting rule is just as short. In a fair snapshot, a longer phase holds more cells.
scenes.caption: The count still teaches an important idea. Cells spend time growing, copying DNA, and preparing before chromosomes visibly separate. That preparation serves the first film's rule. Copy each chromosome first; separate the copies so each nucleus gets one. And the counting rule is just as short. In a fair snapshot, a longer phase holds more cells.
scenes.visual: Return to the root-tip field. Fade most cells into interphase while a smaller group keeps visible chromosomes. Draw the full cycle around the field and highlight preparation before separation. Bring back the small guiding-rule badge from the first film. Then show the two unequal lanes once more beside it, and clear both before the end card.
scenes.narration: The count still teaches an important idea. Cells spend time growing, copying DNA, and preparing before chromosomes visibly separate. That preparation serves the first film's rule. Copy each chromosome first; separate the copies so each nucleus gets one. And the counting rule is just as short. In a fair snapshot, a longer phase holds more cells.

scenes.visual: Clear the frame. Show one centered line only, with no title or smaller text: 'In a fair snapshot, a longer phase holds more cells.'
